newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Colombia favours change in U.S. anti-drug policy.
newsitem.headline: Colombia favours change in U.S. anti-drug policy.

text.p: Colombian President Ernesto Samper on Wednesday applauded an effort by key political figures in the United States to change a controversial practice of certifying countries according to their drug policies.

In February, Washington "decertified" Colombia for the second straight year, saying the home of notorious drug cartels was no ally in the international fight against narcotics. But no economic sanctions have been ordered to back the U.S. censure.

"I am in favour of the initiative to eliminate drug certification. We have been working very closely with the senators and representatives that are promoting this abolition of the certification process," Samper told Reuters in an interview during an official visit to Israel.

Last week, U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich called the certification process "offensive". U.S. drug Czar General Barry McCaffrey said a more multilateral approach would be more effective.
Samper said the certification process divided countries and hindered the cooperation needed to fight the drug trade.

"We believe it is an unfair instrument and goes against what we think must be the way to solve the drug trafficking problem," said Samper, who is on a 10-day tour of Africa and the Middle East that has aroused controversy both at home and in Israel.
In Colombia, the trip was criticised as a waste of time and money and dubbed as little more than an expensive "safari".
In Israel, the Jerusalem Post quoted diplomatic sources as saying Samper's visit to the Jewish state had aroused the displeasure of the United States, where he is suspected of ties to drug barons.
Israel Radio said the United States presented Israel with a list of crimes they suspect Samper committed.

Richard Scorza, spokesman for the U.S. embassy in Tel Aviv, would not comment specifically on any discussions with Israel. But he noted Samper was a "persona non grata" in the United States and ineligible for a U.S. visa.

"We don't have a position on Israel inviting a person. We understand he is the head of the Non-Aligned Movement. We do advise our host countries from time to time about our findings about people who we believe are receiving in this case drug-related campaign contributions," Scorza said.
Commenting on the U.S. entry ban, Samper said: "It is the same as saying, 'Look, I don't want to invite you to my home.'"
U.S. President Bill Clinton would be "very welcome" in Colombia, he said.
Samper dismissed as "ridiculous" an accusation last week from a Colombian legislator that he ordered the murder of a high-profile opposition leader in 1995.
Colombian chief prosecutor's office said the legislator had twisted the facts.
The trip to Israel was aimed at reinforcing economic and military ties, Samper said.
The Colombian Air Force already uses Israeli fighter aircraft and the Latin American nation is interested in future purchases of military supplies, he said.
But on this trip, Samper said he was looking at satellite technology from Israel Aircraft Industries for use in a project to integrate communications in the Andean region.
